About this tool

Not every password that looks complicated is strong. This checker estimates how hard your password would be to guess, shows how long a fast offline attack might take, and points out common mistakes such as repeated characters and keyboard patterns. The password is analyzed in your browser and never leaves it.

How it works

The estimate starts from length and character variety, which gives an entropy figure in bits. It then lowers the score for passwords on a list of very common choices, for repeated characters and for sequences like abc, 123 or qwerty. The crack time assumes an offline attack at 10 billion guesses per second, which is fast but realistic for stolen password databases.

How to use

  1. Type or paste a password to test.
  2. Read the score, the entropy and the tips.
  3. Replace weak passwords, ideally with a randomly generated one.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to type my real password here?

The check runs entirely in your browser and no request is made with your password. Still, it is good practice to test a similar password rather than one you use today.

What does entropy in bits mean?

It measures how many guesses an attacker would need. Each extra bit doubles the work, so 60 bits is roughly a million times harder to guess than 40 bits.

Why is my long password rated weak?

Predictable patterns count against it. Repeated characters, sequences, and common words are tried first by attackers, so the checker reduces the score even when the password is long.

Does this tell me if my password was leaked?

No. This tool estimates guessability only. To see whether an email address or password appeared in a data breach, use a dedicated breach-checking service.

What makes a really strong password?

At least 16 random characters, or a passphrase of several random words, used on one account only and stored in a password manager. Add two-factor authentication where possible.

How accurate is the crack time?

It is a rough estimate. Real attackers use dictionaries and patterns, and the speed depends on how the site stores passwords. Treat it as a way to compare passwords, not as a promise.
